title: Survival Stories in the Wild
objectives: I can explain how animals find food, hide, and stay safe using ten new words.
I can use context clues to figure out what a survival word means.
I can tell about a danger to an animal and how people can help.
I can write sentences that show what an animal does to survive.
rationale: Survival verbs give third graders a cause-and-need story to retell: animals need food, safety, and a place to live, so they forage, scavenge, hide, flee, or migrate. The words split into how animals get what they need (forage, scavenge, prowl, instinct), how they stay safe (camouflage, flee, vanish, migrate), and what puts them at risk (threaten, endangered). Science reading in grades 3 and 4 uses these words constantly, and the unit builds on the forest and weather words students already know.

passage.title: A Winter in the Meadow
paras: Every autumn, the meadow changes. The days grow short, and the air turns cold. Some animals leave. Geese migrate to warmer lakes, flying in long lines across the sky. Other animals stay and must find a way to live through the winter.

Rabbits do not need a teacher. They follow instinct. When an owl's shadow slides over the grass, a rabbit knows to flee. Its brown fur is camouflage against the dry stalks, so the owl often cannot spot it. In a blink, the rabbit can vanish into a hollow log or a thicket.

Night belongs to other animals. A fox will prowl along the old fence, listening for mice. The mice forage in the stubble for seeds, staying close to cover. Crows scavenge whatever food the farmers drop, and they are always watching.

Some meadow birds are now endangered because fields have become roads and parking lots. New buildings can threaten their nests. When people protect a meadow, they protect all of its small survivors, from the tiny mouse to the soaring goose.

qs.q: In paragraph 2, the word "vanish" most nearly means
qs.why: The rabbit slips into a hollow log or thicket, where the owl cannot see it, so vanish means disappear from sight.

qs.q: How does a rabbit know to flee from an owl's shadow?
choices: It follows instinct and is born knowing what to do.
A teacher shows it what to do.

qs.why: The passage says rabbits do not need a teacher and follow instinct.

qs.q: Which detail best shows that crows scavenge?
choices: They fly in long lines across the sky.
They listen for mice along the fence.
They eat whatever food the farmers drop.
qs.why: Scavenging means eating leftovers, and the crows eat food that farmers drop.

qs.q: What is this passage mostly about?
choices: How meadow animals live through winter and what puts them at risk
qs.why: The passage covers how several animals survive and ends with dangers to the meadow.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten survival words, read a short informational passage about a meadow in winter, and use the words to retell how animals find food, stay safe, and face danger.

notes.va.forage.v: Forage is about searching for food in the wild. Compare with scavenge: foragers look for fresh food like seeds and berries; scavengers eat leftovers.
notes.va.instinct.n: Instinct is behavior an animal is born knowing. Ask: could the animal learn this from a teacher? If no, it is probably instinct.
notes.va.camouflage.n: Camouflage helps something blend in. Show two pictures, one hidden and one easy to see, and have students explain the difference.
notes.va.migrate.v: Migrate means a long seasonal trip. Students often say it for any move; use a map to show a real route such as monarchs going to Mexico.
notes.va.scavenge.v: Scavenge is not the same as steal. Scavengers eat food left behind, and many help clean up nature.
notes.va.vanish.v: Vanish means gone from sight, quickly. Link to camouflage: an animal can seem to vanish because it blends in.
notes.va.endangered.adj: Endangered means very few of a kind are left. It is not the same as one animal being hurt. Use the ladder: common, at risk, endangered, extinct.
notes.va.threaten.v: Threaten means to be a danger. Students may think only a person can threaten; show that pollution, storms, and roads can too.
notes.va.prowl.v: Prowl is slow and quiet movement while hunting. Act it out, then compare with stomp from the earlier movement unit.
notes.va.flee.v: Flee is running away from danger. The past form is fled; practice both. Contrast with walk away calmly.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: "The passage says the rabbit's fur is brown like the dry stalks. That helps it hide, so that is camouflage. When the owl's shadow passes, the rabbit runs away fast, so it will flee. I can prove each word with a detail from the text."
